data.name: Breaking Bones
data.detailed_description:
Breaking Bones is a survival game using the technology of photogrammetry (3d scan). It's a First Person Melee game with some shooting component (bow & catapult).





Travel the world through quarries, islands, forests, mountains, deserts and more. Fight skeletons, dragons and dinosaurs. At your disposal a large number of deadly weapons, catapults and bows.

You can pick up weapons from your enemies after their deaths. Each map contains hidden weapons, life potions and explosive barrels.

In each level, there is a wolf in her cage. when you find the key and free him, he will fight at your side.





- 6 maps
- 18 enemies
- 6 boss and 6 big boss
- 20+ weapons
- Catapult
- Wolf

reviews.review:
Breaking Bones is a small-scale first-person survival action game that embraces an unusual mixture of realistic environments and wildly fantastical enemies. Developed and published by Duplicator Studio, it feels more like an experimental indie project than a conventional survival game. Its defining visual idea is the use of photogrammetry and 3D-scanned environments, which gives many locations a grounded, natural appearance. Against these realistic surroundings, the game throws skeletons, dinosaurs, dragons, and other creatures at the player, resulting in an intentionally strange combination that gives the experience much of its personality.

The central gameplay revolves around exploring hostile areas while surviving encounters through melee and ranged combat. There are more than twenty weapons to discover and use, providing enough variety to encourage experimentation. Weapons can be obtained from defeated enemies or discovered while searching the environment, making exploration worthwhile rather than purely optional. Bows and catapults supplement close-range equipment and give players additional ways of approaching dangerous creatures. The mechanics are not especially elaborate, but the broad assortment of equipment prevents every encounter from following exactly the same pattern.

Breaking Bones spreads its action across six maps featuring distinctly different environments, including forests, mountains, deserts, islands, and quarry-like areas. The relatively small number of maps limits the overall scale, but the environmental variation keeps progression from becoming visually monotonous too quickly. Players are encouraged to search these areas for concealed weapons and life potions while remaining alert for enemies. Explosive barrels can also be used to deal damage, introducing a simple environmental combat element that rewards awareness of the surroundings.

Enemy variety is one of the game's more entertaining qualities. Eighteen enemy types are accompanied by several bosses and larger confrontations, creating a progression from ordinary encounters toward more dangerous battles. There is little concern for maintaining a realistic theme, and that actually works in the game's favor. Fighting skeletons before confronting dinosaurs or dragons makes each map feel unpredictable. At the same time, players expecting sophisticated enemy behavior or highly technical combat should temper their expectations. The attraction comes more from the eccentric collection of opponents than from advanced artificial intelligence or deeply layered fighting mechanics.

A particularly memorable feature involves rescuing a wolf imprisoned somewhere within each level. Finding the necessary key and freeing the animal gives exploration an additional purpose, after which the wolf can accompany the player and assist during combat. It is a simple feature, but it provides both a practical advantage and a welcome sense of companionship in otherwise hostile environments. This mechanic also helps distinguish exploration from merely searching for health items and stronger equipment.

Despite being described through survival-oriented ideas, Breaking Bones should not be approached as an extensive survival simulator. Its emphasis is much more firmly placed on exploration and combat than on complex crafting, building, hunger management, or long-term character progression. The systems are intentionally straightforward, making the game accessible but also limiting its depth. Once players become accustomed to its weapons, enemy behavior, and map structure, there are fewer additional mechanics waiting to substantially change the experience.

The visual presentation is interesting precisely because it can feel inconsistent. Photogrammetry allows portions of the terrain to appear surprisingly natural, while creatures and other assets can have a noticeably different visual character. This occasionally creates a mismatched appearance, but it also contributes to the game's peculiar charm. Breaking Bones does not resemble a carefully standardized blockbuster production, and players who enjoy unusual independent experiments may find that roughness appealing rather than distracting.

The game is designed for single-player play, fitting its compact structure well. There is no need to organize multiplayer sessions or depend on other players, allowing the experience to be tackled entirely at one's own pace. Its straightforward objectives also make it relatively easy to understand: explore each location, gather useful equipment and health supplies, rescue the wolf when possible, defeat enemies, and overcome the major encounters.

Steam Deck compatibility is not officially verified or rated by Valve on the Steam store listing. Because of that, Breaking Bones should be considered to have an unknown or unsupported official Steam Deck status rather than being described as Verified or Playable. It may still be possible to run the game through SteamOS and Proton, but functionality, controls, performance, and stability cannot be guaranteed from an official compatibility designation. Players purchasing specifically for Steam Deck should therefore expect that manual configuration or experimentation could be necessary.

Breaking Bones ultimately succeeds more as a quirky independent action experiment than as a deep survival experience. Its combination of scanned landscapes, varied weapons, hidden equipment, explosive environmental objects, rescuable wolves, dinosaurs, skeletons, dragons, and boss encounters creates an identity that is difficult to mistake for something else. The limited amount of content and relatively basic mechanics hold it back from providing substantial longevity, yet there is entertainment to be found in its unpredictability and unconventional design. Players interested in obscure first-person indie games may appreciate its peculiar collection of ideas, while anyone expecting extensive survival systems or highly polished combat will likely find it too modest.

Its unusual environments, bizarre enemy selection, weapon variety, exploration incentives, and wolf companion mechanic make it an interesting curiosity, but limited depth, modest production values, and uncertain Steam Deck support keep it from achieving broader appeal.

Rating: 5/10
